teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose baseline A and candidate B were evaluated on the same 100 orders. Under the supplied probabilities and costs, their expected costs are 0.32 and 0.28. Candidate C reports 0.20 but comes from a different cohort; it is not comparable evidence for this selection. Check B against the predeclared operating and quality limits before ranking it. Keep the confusion-table denominators and fixed cost inputs in the comparison record so another engineer can reproduce the quantities. Do not choose a different deployment prevalence merely because it improves one candidate's result. Protected-test observations remain outside preprocessing fit, candidate choice and tuning; this is a validation decision, not a rehearsal on the protected test.

Make exclusions explicit in the ranking record. Excluding C for its different cohort is not the same as measuring C and finding that it loses. Likewise, an operating-limit failure removes eligibility rather than adding an informal penalty to a quality score. The remaining records can be compared under the fixed criterion because their evidence is matched and their decision inputs agree. Retain the selected candidate identity with the calculated quantities and eligibility results, so later stages know precisely which system the validation choice describes. The protected test remains a separate final check after this selection has been frozen.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: The smallest number in a table is not necessarily the eligible winner. Matched cohorts and fixed requirements are part of the comparison, not details to check after selecting a favorite.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the supplied long-distance group contains 20 eligible orders and eight errors. Its conditional error proportion is 8/20 = 0.40. Compare that evidence with the same-cohort reference for this group, not with a reference measured on unrelated traffic. Inspect the failure observations and any required numerical summaries, retaining the selected observations and standard-deviation divisor. A group with eight errors out of 200 would tell a different story despite the same error count. The purpose of this bounded analysis is to locate an observed failure in the supplied evidence, not claim a cause that has not been tested or treat the developer's preferred examples as the population.

Error inspection should preserve the definition of the failure group. The 20 eligible long-distance observations are the population conditioning this ratio; eight is the count of errors within it. Moving the group boundary after reading failures would answer a different question from the predefined slice. Inspect the supplied example failures for supported task limitations, but distinguish observation from causal explanation. A descriptive feature mean or spread can characterize the selected evidence without proving why predictions failed. Keep the same-cohort reference visible so the localized result is comparable rather than a story based only on a few personally chosen examples.

teaching_blocks.content: A model improves overall, but the team requires separate evidence for predefined delivery zones. Slice evaluation asks the same quality question within each specified segment and keeps its observation count visible.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule

teaching_blocks.content: Compute the arithmetic mean with np.mean(numeric_values) over the selected numeric observations. teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose zone A has two errors among 40 eligible examples and zone B has six among 20. Their observed error proportions are 0.05 and 0.30. Retain both counts rather than reporting only the percentages. Summarize selected numerical observations with the required mean and spread, making clear which slice those observations belong to. Compare the model's supported segment evidence with its overall record without assuming one replaces the other. If the sample does not represent the intended population, these observed differences do not establish a population-level disparity. The result should say what was measured in these slices and what remains unsupported beyond them.

When presenting slices, keep the group labels, eligible counts and quality definition together. Zone A's 0.05 and zone B's 0.30 are conditional sample results, not interchangeable with overall error. Their denominators also reveal that the two estimates come from different numbers of observations. Report supported limitations in the same terms as the supplied evaluation rather than extrapolating beyond the represented population. Numerical feature summaries describe the selected slice values and need their own observation definition. Slice analysis complements aggregate comparison by exposing where the observed task behavior differs; it does not replace the fixed acceptance rule or prove an unmeasured population effect.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Overall improvement is compatible with uneven slice performance. Conversely, an observed sample difference is not by itself proof of a disparity across the whole intended population.

media.group_title: Overall improvement and uneven slice performance

segments.label: How overall improvement hides language-slice gaps
segments.summary: In this synthetic example, underlying fraud is equally common across languages. An English-centric description-quality score is lower for Hindi and Hinglish descriptions, and adding it improves overall fraud detection. The highest-scoring 10% of cases are flagged. Regional flag rates look nearly identical because languages are distributed evenly across regions. Language-specific detection tells a different story: the model detects 33.5% of fraud overall, but only about one-fifth of English-language fraud, over 40% of Hindi-language fraud, and more than half of Hinglish-language fraud. Overall improvement therefore coexists with uneven slice performance, including missed English-language fraud and burdens on innocent Hindi- and Hinglish-speaking customers.

bridge_note.before: Watch how similar regional flag rates conceal different language-specific fraud detection rates. These are distinct measurements in a synthetic example; overall improvement does not guarantee consistent performance across slices.
bridge_note.after: The clip demonstrates uneven slice performance, but does not provide eligible counts, explain population representativeness, or teach NumPy mean and standard deviation. The text supplies those reporting requirements, limitations, and calculations.

required_facts.statement: For binary validation counts, FPR = FP/(FP+TN) conditions on actual negatives, and FNR = FN/(FN+TP) conditions on actual positives; an empty conditioning group does not yield a defined rate.

teaching_blocks.title: Errors, Slices and Subgroup Risks
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied mitigation targets a subgroup with a poor validation result. Check whether the data represents that group, then evaluate the mitigation on both the affected segment and the overall cohort. Do not assume changing the model is the only explanation or remedy.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Evaluate whether the data represents the groups for which the model is intended before attributing a subgroup problem solely to the model. Check the supplied mitigation on the affected validation segment as well as the overall validation cohort before accepting it. For a subgroup, its contribution to total expected harm is its deployment population probability multiplied by its subgroup-conditional expected harm; use the supplied error costs for that calculation.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: For binary validation counts, FPR = FP/(FP+TN) conditions on actual negatives, and FNR = FN/(FN+TP) conditions on actual positives; an empty conditioning group does not yield a defined rate.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the deployment probability of the subgroup is 0.25 and its subgroup-conditional expected harm under the supplied error costs is 0.80. Its contribution to total expected harm is 0.25 × 0.80 = 0.20. If a supplied mitigation changes the subgroup harm to 0.60, the corresponding contribution becomes 0.15 under the same population probability. Still inspect its overall validation evidence and the affected group's representation before accepting it. For any binary-rate calculation, retain the actual-negative and actual-positive denominators separately. The calculation weights conditional harm by population share; it does not turn a small evaluation sample into justified deployment representation.

The multiplication by 0.25 is the population weighting step, not a revision to the subgroup's conditional rate. Keep subgroup false-positive and false-negative conditions distinct when computing its harm. Then compare the supplied mitigation with the reference on a matched affected segment and overall cohort. An improvement in the subgroup contribution is useful evidence only under the supplied population probability and cost assumptions. Inspect representation before extending that evidence to deployment. The exercise is a bounded check of a provided mitigation; it does not authorize inventing protected categories, new policies or an untested repair that merely seems fair.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A subgroup-only improvement is not sufficient acceptance evidence. Population probability, conditional harm and representation are distinct parts of the evaluation, and empty conditioning groups do not provide error rates.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose features have shape (4, 2), and the declared targets have shape (4,). Construct tensors from the two NumPy arrays, explicitly convert each to its declared dtype, and inspect the resulting shapes and dtypes. Return the aligned pair as a tuple only after checking the common batch length and required axes. A target fixture with three rows fails correspondence even if each target value is individually permitted. Another fixture can test an incorrect declared target representation without changing the feature dtype. Keeping these checks separate makes it clear whether a failure concerns feature shape, target shape, dtype or matching observations, rather than reporting only that conversion succeeded.

Inspect features and targets separately before checking their common observation axis. A classification target representation may differ from numerical features, so an explicit cast should use the target's declared dtype rather than a shared convenience setting. Return the pair only after the axes and representations satisfy the contract. In the three-target failure fixture, tensor conversion may still succeed; the alignment check is what rejects it. Test that failure alongside an accepted pair and the supplied boundary. This establishes a reliable input contract for later minibatch use without relying on a subsequent loss to expose an earlier conversion error.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Constructing tensors does not establish their task contract. Target dtype must come from the declared target representation, and equal-looking values do not repair a mismatched batch length.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For five indexed observations and batch_size 2, a fixture with drop_last=False retains batches of sizes 2, 2 and 1. With drop_last=True, it retains two complete batches and discards the incomplete final batch. Retrieve each feature and target from the same observation index in __getitem__, and return them together. Test the batch boundaries and observed pairings under the declared shuffle policy rather than assuming a loader output's first position still corresponds to the source's first row. Also check __len__ against the sample count. The choice about the incomplete batch must appear in the fixture expectations, because counting three batches of size two would invent an observation.

Indexing defines correspondence before batching. If __getitem__ uses the feature at one index and the target at another, a loader can still collate a well-shaped but incorrectly paired batch. Test item identities as well as batch dimensions. The five-observation fixture also exposes the final partial-batch policy: retaining it gives one smaller batch, while dropping it changes how much of the dataset is consumed. Shuffle governs order, not whether a feature and its target remain the same item. Keep these responsibilities distinct so the expected loader output is tied to the dataset contract rather than assumed from its shape alone.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A minibatch loader does not make a partial batch full. Dropping or retaining the final incomplete batch is an explicit policy, and feature/target alignment begins with the dataset item.

context.concept_name: Define a neural network with task-compatible layers and activations

coverage.learning_objective: Build a minimal module whose layer widths, nonlinearity and output shape satisfy the task.

required_facts.statement: Import torch.nn as nn and define an nn.Module subclass with super().__init__(), registered layer attributes and a forward(self, x) method.
nn.Linear(in_features, out_features) maps each input feature vector to out_features outputs using learned weights and bias, preserving the leading minibatch dimension.
nn.ReLU applies max(0, x) elementwise and introduces a nonlinearity between linear layers.
nn.Sequential composes its modules in declared order; match each layer’s output width to the next layer’s input width.
Set the final layer width and activation to the supplied output task contract and verify the resulting output shape with a fixture batch.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose a fixture has four observations with two features, and the declared model uses widths 2 → 3 → 1. The first linear layer maps each two-feature vector to three outputs; ReLU applies its elementwise nonlinearity; the final linear layer maps three to one. The expected output shape is (4, 1), preserving the minibatch length. Register layers as attributes in an nn.Module subclass and implement forward, or use the supplied Sequential composition. Verify the final activation against the task contract rather than adding one from habit. A width mismatch between the intermediate output and the next input is a contract problem, not something a different batch size fixes.

Draw or inspect the dimension chain for a single observation and then restore the leading minibatch dimension. Two features enter the first layer, three intermediate values emerge and one final output is produced; all four observations follow the same chain. Registered layer attributes make those layer parameters part of the module. The activation is elementwise, so it changes values without changing that intermediate width. Finally, compare the model output with the declared target/loss contract. The architecture example remains bounded to that contract rather than adding layers or final nonlinearities simply because they appear in another task.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Linear layer widths describe per-observation feature/output dimensions, not the number of observations. The final width and activation come from the supplied task rather than a generic neural-network template.

context.concept_name: Compute neural-network gradients with automatic differentiation

coverage.learning_objective: Verify parameter gradients against the corresponding matrix-shaped derivative reference.

required_facts.statement: Autograd records tensor operations as a computation graph and differentiates the scalar output through that graph using the chain rule.
source_refs: pytorch_learn_basics#autogradqs_tutorial.html — Tensors, Functions and Computational graph; Computing Gradients

required_facts.statement: Set requires_grad=True on trainable leaf tensors, form the supplied scalar loss, call loss.backward(), and inspect each leaf parameter’s .grad.
source_refs: pytorch_learn_basics#autogradqs_tutorial.html — Tensors, Functions and Computational graph; Computing Gradients

required_facts.statement: Backward accumulates into .grad, so clear old gradients before comparing a fresh computation with the reference.
source_refs: pytorch_learn_basics#autogradqs_tutorial.html — Tensors, Functions and Computational graph; Computing Gradients

required_facts.statement: For a linear batch Z = XW + b with scalar-loss derivative D = ∂L/∂Z, the chain rule yields ∂L/∂W = X.T @ D and ∂L/∂b = D.sum(axis=0), with any loss reduction already included in D.
source_refs: pytorch_learn_basics#autogradqs_tutorial.html — Tensors, Functions and Computational graph; Computing Gradients

required_facts.statement: Compare the computed gradients to the matrix-shaped chain-rule reference with explicit relative and absolute tolerances.
Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.content: A scalar loss must send the intended learning signal through the linear computation to its parameters. Autograd's result is inspectable: compare parameter gradients with a matrix-shaped chain-rule reference, not just with an expectation that backward should work.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Autograd records tensor operations as a computation graph and differentiates the scalar output through that graph using the chain rule. Backward accumulates into .grad, so clear old gradients before comparing a fresh computation with the reference.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: For a linear batch Z = XW + b with scalar-loss derivative D = ∂L/∂Z, the chain rule yields ∂L/∂W = X.T @ D and ∂L/∂b = D.sum(axis=0), with any loss reduction already included in D. Compare the computed gradients to the matrix-shaped chain-rule reference with explicit relative and absolute tolerances. Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Take X=[[1, 2], [3, 4]] and the supplied derivative D=[[0.1], [0.2]] for Z=XW+b. The weight-gradient reference is X.T @ D = [[0.7], [1.0]], and the bias-gradient reference is [0.3]. Any loss reduction is already included in D; dividing again would change the reference. Set trainable leaf tensors to require gradients, form the scalar loss and call backward. Inspect .grad before clearing it, and compare shapes and values under explicit tolerances. For a fresh computation, clear the old gradients first because backward accumulates. Include a failure fixture whose gradient differs from the declared reference, not only a successful call.

Read the matrix reference one parameter at a time. The first weight combines feature values 1 and 3 with derivatives 0.1 and 0.2, giving 0.7. The second combines 2 and 4 with the same derivatives, giving 1.0. The bias combines derivatives over rows, giving 0.3. These shapes are part of the check: a transpose error can yield a different object even when some scalar values look plausible. Because D includes the loss reduction, use it once as supplied. Compare after backward and before clearing so the inspected gradients correspond to the intended fresh computation rather than zeroed or accumulated state.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Backward does not overwrite every old gradient automatically. A gradient comparison also needs the correct matrix shapes and reduction convention; a numerically plausible scalar is not the weight matrix reference.

media.group_title: How autograd carries derivatives through a computation graph

segments.label: Trace a scalar tensor computation and inspect its gradient
segments.summary: PyTorch tracks operations on a tensor when requires_grad=True. Starting with a three-element tensor x, the demonstration forms y = x + 2, multiplies y by itself and by 2, and takes the mean to produce a scalar. Each tracked operation contributes to a computation graph and has an associated gradient function. Calling backward() on the scalar computes its derivative with respect to x and stores the result in x.grad. Repeating the construction without enabling gradient tracking leads to an error when backward() is called. The explanation connects differentiation through the graph to the chain rule: local derivatives are combined to obtain the final gradient. Because the output is scalar, this backward() call needs no explicit gradient argument.

bridge_note.before: Watch how tracked operations connect a tensor to a scalar output and how backward() populates its gradient. The clip uses “computational graph”; Devspace calls this a computation graph.
bridge_note.after: The clip demonstrates the mechanism, not the complete parameter-verification contract. The text adds the supplied-loss leaf-parameter workflow, gradient clearing, matrix references, explicit tolerances, and valid, boundary, and failure assertions.

context.concept_name: Choose a task-compatible training loss

coverage.learning_objective: Choose a task-compatible loss and verify its output, target and gradient contracts.

required_facts.statement: A loss compares model outputs with the corresponding target representation; choose its input contract before computing the scalar objective.
source_refs: pytorch_learn_basics#optimization_tutorial.html — Hyperparameters; Loss Function; Optimizer; Full Implementation

required_facts.statement: CrossEntropyLoss expects unnormalized class logits; for class-index targets, logits have shape (N, C), targets have shape (N,) with dtype long and values in [0, C).
MSELoss takes input and target tensors of the same shape and, under mean reduction, averages their squared elementwise differences.
BCEWithLogitsLoss combines sigmoid and binary cross-entropy for logits and same-shaped targets in [0, 1], rather than expecting already-sigmoid-transformed inputs.

For mean squared error over M output elements, the loss derivative with respect to an output is 2 × (output−target)/M, so its sign points toward increasing loss as the output moves away from the target.
For unweighted mean binary cross-entropy with logits over M elements, the logit derivative is (sigmoid(logit)−target)/M; this distinguishes the probability representation from the raw logit.

For mean class-index cross-entropy without weighting, the derivative per sample logit is (softmax probability−one-hot target)/N, so output width, target identity and reduction affect the gradient reference.

teaching_blocks.title: Gradients, Loss and Optimizer
teaching_blocks.content: The model output and target must meet the selected loss's contract. A scalar loss value alone cannot tell you whether class indices, logits, probabilities and same-shaped numerical targets were used correctly.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: A loss compares model outputs with the corresponding target representation; choose its input contract before computing the scalar objective. CrossEntropyLoss expects unnormalized class logits; for class-index targets, logits have shape (N, C), targets have shape (N,) with dtype long and values in [0, C). MSELoss takes input and target tensors of the same shape and, under mean reduction, averages their squared elementwise differences.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: BCEWithLogitsLoss combines sigmoid and binary cross-entropy for logits and same-shaped targets in [0, 1], rather than expecting already-sigmoid-transformed inputs. For mean squared error over M output elements, the loss derivative with respect to an output is 2 × (output−target)/M, so its sign points toward increasing loss as the output moves away from the target. For unweighted mean binary cross-entropy with logits over M elements, the logit derivative is (sigmoid(logit)−target)/M; this distinguishes the probability representation from the raw logit.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: For mean class-index cross-entropy without weighting, the derivative per sample logit is (softmax probability−one-hot target)/N, so output width, target identity and reduction affect the gradient reference.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For an unweighted mean squared-error fixture with outputs [2, 4] and targets [1, 2], the loss is (1²+2²)/2 = 2.5 and output derivatives are [1, 2]. For a binary-logit fixture with one logit 0 and target 1, sigmoid(0)=0.5, so the supplied mean-logit derivative is −0.5. For target 1, decreasing the logit increases loss, while increasing it decreases loss. For a class-index task with three classes, verify logits width 3 and long target indices in [0, 3); use the stated softmax-minus-one-hot reference with its sample-count reduction. These are distinct output contracts, not interchangeable wrappers around arbitrary tensors.

Keep the mean-reduction factor visible in each reference. The two-element MSE fixture divides squared errors by two, while the one-element binary-logit fixture divides its sigmoid-minus-target derivative by one. A class-index cross-entropy reference subtracts the one-hot target from the softmax vector and divides by the sample count. Those equations support different target representations, so verify target dtype and axes before applying them. A positive-looking scalar loss is not proof of the right contract. Compare both value and derivative direction in the bounded fixture, retaining the supplied assumptions about unweighted mean reduction.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: CrossEntropyLoss expects unnormalized logits for the class-index case; BCEWithLogitsLoss also expects logits, not already-sigmoid inputs. MSE's same-shape contract must be checked rather than left to accidental broadcasting.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For plain SGD with no momentum, weight decay or other modifications, let a parameter be 2, its current gradient 3 and learning rate 0.1. The reference new value is 2 − 0.1 × 3 = 1.7, with change −0.3. Clear old gradients, compute backward and then step. Retain the before and after values and compare their difference with the reference under declared tolerances. Initialize the optimizer with model.parameters() so it acts on the supplied trainable model parameters. A fixture that calls backward but never step would produce a gradient without this parameter update. Keep the plain-SGD restrictions visible so this arithmetic is not mistaken for the update rule of every optimizer.

Retain the current gradient separately from the observed parameter change. The former is produced by backward; the latter is produced by step acting on the parameters bound to the optimizer. A parameter change of −0.3 matches the plain-SGD reference for gradient 3 and rate 0.1, but the same number alone would not identify what happened if those inputs differed. Check before/after values and declared tolerances together. Clearing gradients before the next backward prevents previous contributions from altering the intended fresh-step reference. Keep this one-step verification bounded to the stated optimizer configuration rather than extending its equation to Adam.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A learning rate alone does not cause learning; the current backward result must reach step. The plain-SGD equation is conditional on its stated lack of momentum, weight decay and other modifications.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
With five observations and retained batches of sizes 2, 2 and 1, compute model outputs and loss for each aligned feature/target pair. For every minibatch, zero gradients, backpropagate that batch's loss and apply the optimizer step. Collect scalar loss.item() values with batch counts, so an epoch summary does not pretend all batches contain two observations. In the deterministic plain-SGD fixture, retain the pre-step parameter and compare its observed change with −learning_rate × current_gradient under tolerance. Test the loop's supplied valid, boundary and failure cases. The repeated sequence is what links each batch to its intended current gradient, rather than using an accumulated leftover from another batch.

Loss aggregation needs the accompanying batch counts because the last one-observation batch does not contribute the same number of examples as a two-observation batch. Record each scalar with its batch size before applying the declared epoch-summary rule. The loop's nested structure is equally important: each epoch iterates its loader, and each minibatch performs the complete current-gradient update sequence. A step outside the intended minibatch position would define a different training procedure. The deterministic fixture can inspect one update within the loop, making the control flow and parameter-change evidence meet at the same minibatch.

teaching_blocks.content: An epoch is not just a count of calls to step. Batch sizes affect how a loss summary is interpreted, and old gradients must not silently become part of the next minibatch's intended update.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For a dropout fixture with p=0.5, training randomly masks elements and doubles retained values. Evaluation returns the input unchanged. Test the masking/scaling rule without assuming every random training call must mask at least one element. Wrap validation in no_grad and set eval; a no_grad-only training-mode dropout fixture can still use dropout behavior. Keep validation forward-only, with no optimizer step, and restore train before the next training pass. This makes the fixture demonstrate why an evaluation-mode switch and a gradient-recording switch address different concerns. Compare expected evaluation output and the permitted training outcomes, not one arbitrarily expected random mask.

Training mode and gradient recording can be considered independently in the fixture. Evaluation-mode dropout behaves as an identity even if graph recording is enabled. Training-mode dropout can still mask values while no_grad is active. Neither observation alone describes the whole validation procedure, which also excludes parameter updates. Inspect the layer output and the chosen context separately, then restore training mode before returning to the training loop. This avoids interpreting a stochastic dropout value as a prediction-quality problem or assuming that a disabled graph has also changed layer behavior.

teaching_blocks.content: eval does not disable graph recording, and no_grad does not switch dropout to evaluation behavior. Validation also must not update parameters just because a gradient context was disabled.

media.group_title: Separate layer mode from gradient recording

segments.label: Training and validation use two independent controls
segments.summary: Use model.train() before parameter training and model.eval() before validation. These settings change the behavior of layers such as dropout and batch normalization; leaving training behavior active can introduce unwanted variability into validation scores. Separately, wrap validation computation in torch.no_grad() to prevent gradient graph recording. Evaluation mode controls layer behavior, not graph recording. Each training epoch begins by restoring training mode, computing the forward pass and loss, clearing gradients, running backward, and stepping the optimizer. The separate validation block switches to evaluation mode and computes validation loss inside no_grad without updating parameters. Recording both losses keeps the training and validation measurements distinct.

context.concept_name: Stop training using validation behavior without consulting the protected test

coverage.learning_objective: Implement a validation-patience controller that returns the best retained model state.

required_facts.statement: Predeclare the validation quantity, improvement direction, minimum improvement and patience; patience counts consecutive epochs without sufficient improvement.
For a minimized validation quantity, reset the non-improvement counter only when current < best − min_delta; otherwise increment it and stop when the declared patience is exhausted.
Retain the model weights associated with the best monitored validation value rather than automatically using the last epoch’s weights.
A state_dict refers to live parameter values, so preserve a best-epoch state with a deep copy or a saved state file before later updates alter the model.
Do not use protected test observations to fit preprocessing, choose a model or tune its settings; doing so leaks information into the chosen system.
Implement the controller as a while loop bounded by maximum epochs and the non-improvement rule; update best loss/checkpoint inside the improvement branch and use break when patience is exhausted.
source_refs: python_tutorial#controlflow.html — Defining Functions; Default Argument Values; Keyword Arguments

teaching_blocks.title: Stop and Debug Training
teaching_blocks.content: A validation quantity improves and then stalls. Early stopping is a predeclared controller over this sequence, not a decision to use whichever epoch happened to run last. Preserve the best checkpoint accepted under the declared minimum-improvement rule while training can still alter live parameters.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Predeclare the validation quantity, improvement direction, minimum improvement and patience; patience counts consecutive epochs without sufficient improvement. For a minimized validation quantity, reset the non-improvement counter only when current < best − min_delta; otherwise increment it and stop when the declared patience is exhausted. Here, best is the validation value at the most recent checkpoint accepted under min_delta, not necessarily the lowest observed value. Retain that accepted checkpoint’s model weights rather than automatically using the last epoch’s weights.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: A state_dict refers to live parameter values, so preserve a best-epoch state with a deep copy or a saved state file before later updates alter the model. Do not use protected test observations to fit preprocessing, choose a model or tune its settings; doing so leaks information into the chosen system. Implement the controller as a while loop bounded by maximum epochs and the non-improvement rule; update best loss/checkpoint inside the improvement branch and use break when patience is exhausted.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose minimized validation values are 0.50, 0.44, 0.43 and 0.45, with min_delta 0.02 and patience 2. The move from 0.50 to 0.44 is sufficient improvement and resets the counter. The value 0.43 does not satisfy 0.43 < 0.44−0.02, so the counter becomes one; 0.45 makes it two and exhausts patience. The lowest observed value is 0.43, but the best checkpoint accepted under min_delta is the one at 0.44. Retain the 0.44 checkpoint’s weights, preserving them by deep copy or a saved state file. Bound the while loop by maximum epochs as well as the non-improvement rule. Protected-test observations do not decide patience or checkpoint choice.

Trace the controller's counter explicitly after every validation value. Reset only when the minimized quantity improves by more than min_delta, increment otherwise and stop when patience is exhausted or the epoch bound is reached. teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the derivative reference predicts a negative gradient for a selected parameter, but the reproduced record shows zero. Inspect .grad after backward and before clearing it, then follow the derivative chain from loss through outputs to that parameter. Check the target representation and declared learning rate alongside the loss computation. Choose one supported root-cause hypothesis, apply its supplied correction and rerun the identical bounded fixture. Compare the corrected loss and gradient signs and magnitudes with the failing reference. A lower loss in a different task or with multiple simultaneous changes would not isolate this hypothesis. Keep assertion fixtures for both the expected computation and the reproduced failure.

The identical rerun is what makes the correction test informative. Preserve the fixture, target contract and baseline failing evidence while changing the one supported factor. If the correction is intended to restore a missing gradient path, inspect the derivative and parameter .grad at the same points as before. If the supplied cause concerns representation or learning rate, retain those resolved inputs in the comparison. Record whether the corrected bounded task meets its declared expectations, not just whether an exception disappeared. This isolates evidence for one hypothesis without claiming that all future training failures have the same cause.

Change one supported bottleneck factor and compare the same bounded workload again rather than inferring improvement only from a code change. Inspect CPU and memory measurements and running process state during the profiled interval, using docker stats and docker top for a containerized run, to distinguish resource limits from stage timing evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Warm up the bounded workload, then profile its labeled regions. If the trace attributes most measured work to loading, test one supported loading factor rather than immediately changing model computation. Inspect CPU, memory and process state during the same interval; for the container fixture, docker stats and docker top provide that supporting evidence. After the change, compare the same bounded workload again without profiler overhead in the final timing. On CUDA, synchronize measurement boundaries so a CPU clock includes completed accelerator work. Keep the profiling attribution separate from the final unprofiled performance comparison, since they answer related but different questions.

The profiler trace supplies attribution, while the unprofiled rerun supplies the matched elapsed-time comparison. Keep the same bounded workload and one-factor change between those two comparisons. A loading-region label should enclose the intended loading work; a model-compute label should identify that separate work rather than blend it with setup. Runtime CPU, memory and process evidence must refer to the same window. Synchronization at accelerator timing boundaries accounts for asynchronous completion. This makes the observed difference interpretable without assuming that a profiler's overhead or a shifted measurement boundary is a genuine speed improvement.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A code change is not evidence of improvement. Asynchronous accelerator work and profiler overhead can alter timing interpretation unless the measurement boundaries and final comparison are controlled.

media.group_title: Make direct execution explicit with an entry-point guard

segments.label: Guard a Python entry point so importing the module does not call it
segments.summary: Python assigns __name__ the value "__main__" when a file runs directly. When another file imports that module, __name__ instead identifies the imported module. The demonstration first leaves diagnostic output at module level, where it executes during import. It then moves that output into a main function and calls the function behind if __name__ == "__main__":. Direct execution calls main; importing the module does not. The guard controls the entry-point call, not every statement in the file.

bridge_note.before: Watch how direct execution and importing assign different values to __name__. The creator calls the entry function a “main method”; here, it is a Python function.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Upload the supplied dataset to the version-enabled test bucket and record its created generation and the SHA-256 digest of the local bytes. Later, select that recorded generation explicitly, verify it exists and download it. Compare the downloaded bytes' digest with the expected snapshot identity. In the authorized overwrite fixture, change only the mutable latest object, then retrieve the original generation again. The observed original digest should still match the snapshot record. Keep object name, generation and digest together: the name tells you which object family, the generation selects the version, and the digest checks the bytes you actually obtained.

The overwrite test separates immutable snapshot selection from the mutable object's current state. Verify the recorded generation exists before relying on it, and check the content after retrieval rather than assuming a version-qualified request returned the expected bytes. A local digest computed before upload and a digest of the later download can be compared directly as content evidence. Keep the selected generation in the record even when both old and latest objects happen to have the same name. The test proves retrieval of the recorded fixture, not a claim that mutable names are intrinsically safe for reproduction.

teaching_blocks.content: A mutable object name is not immutable data identity. Recording a digest without verifying downloaded bytes also does not establish that the intended snapshot was retrieved.

A numeric boundary fixture can test an included limit and a value just beyond it. Send the serialized body as encoded bytes with the declared JSON header and a bounded timeout, decode the returned JSON and inspect its fields. Parsing success, request validity and response correctness are three different checks; retain each failure explicitly rather than returning a successful result for malformed input.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose five keyed orders are processed in chunks of two, two and one. Apply the fitted preprocessing and model to each chunk, keeping each order key with its prediction. Write that bounded set of serialized results before reading the next chunk. Decode the written fixture again and verify its schema and one-result-per-eligible-key correspondence. A missing key or duplicate output is a failure even if the total number of rows looks reasonable. Keep explicit input and output handles and the declared reader format. The procedure is inference over chunks, not fitting a new model or preprocessor for whichever chunk happens to arrive next.

Keep an output key beside its prediction through serialization, not merely in a temporary input structure. After writing, decode the fixture and compare key coverage against the eligible input IDs. A duplicate result for A plus a missing result for B could leave the total row count unchanged, which is why correspondence needs more than counting rows. Each chunk uses the same fitted objects and declared response schema. The bounded writer and reader handles establish where results were produced and re-inspected. This completes an inference path whose correctness includes persistence and identity, not only in-memory prediction values.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A matching total row count does not guarantee one result for every eligible input key. Batch inference preserves keys and fitted state, rather than relying on incidental output order.

teaching_blocks.content: In the prescribed probe, send one valid request per second in [t0, t0+300 seconds), retaining all 300 attempts. Connection refusal and timeouts remain in the denominator even if the handler has no record of them. Allow the final request its whole deadline before summarizing. Instrument JSON decoding, prediction and response encoding, including handled errors, and retain timestamped durations in one unit. Reconcile missing handler records against the external failures instead of computing apparent availability only from requests that arrived.

teaching_blocks.content: Handler success rate is not automatically client-visible availability. Excluding attempts that never reached the handler would omit part of the prescribed denominator and conceal failures.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose one request starts at time 1.0, waits until 1.4 for its batch and completes at 1.6. Its end-to-end duration is 0.6 seconds, not the 0.2-second post-wait interval. Decode the successful response and associate it with the request identity and batching setting. Compute the declared tail percentile, mean and specified spread over the eligible successful-response durations in one unit. Compare settings using the same trace and population interpretation, then choose only a limit satisfying the supplied latency objective. Keep the successful-response sample count visible rather than treating a duration list as if it included failures or unmatched responses.

Use a timeline for the same identified request to avoid measuring different intervals under different settings. Start-to-response timing includes the waiting interval, and the selected successful-response population determines which durations enter the percentile. Record the sample count, units and percentile convention so the numerical summary is reproducible. A limit that reduces model-execution time but increases waiting may fail the full latency objective. The supplied trace is evidence about those measured settings and eligible responses; it does not authorize inventing an unmeasured batching configuration or treating unmatched responses as valid duration samples.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Batch waiting belongs in the stated end-to-end latency. A faster execution interval alone does not make a batching limit acceptable under the full request objective.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the reference has category counts 60 and 40, while the production window has counts 30 and 70, each out of 100. Their aligned proportions are [0.60, 0.40] and [0.30, 0.70]. For numerical features, use the same fixed histogram edges and divide each window's counts by its eligible observation count. Record reference identity, production window and selected means and standard deviations with the specified divisor. A 200-observation window needs its own denominator, not the reference total. This record supports investigation of a distribution change; it does not yet claim that labeled prediction errors increased.

Fixed bins make numerical proportions refer to the same intervals in both windows. The eligible denominator also matters if values outside the declared eligible set are handled explicitly by the reference constraints. context.concept_name: Distinguish data drift, concept drift and observed quality degradation

coverage.learning_objective: Distinguish input shift, changed target relationship and label-supported quality degradation.

required_facts.statement: Input data drift is a change in the observed input distribution relative to its reference; input drift monitoring alone does not measure labeled prediction quality.

teaching_blocks.content: Without matched available labels, report the supported distribution or service evidence and the unresolved quality question rather than asserting labeled quality degradation. teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose a production window contains more long-distance orders than the reference. That is evidence about P(X), the input distribution. It does not establish that P(Y|X), the target relationship conditional on features, changed. To claim observed quality degradation, compare predictions with their corresponding ground truth and the declared quality reference. If matched available labels are absent, record the supported distribution or service observation and the unresolved quality question. Conversely, a conditional target relationship can change in the concept-drift sense even when an input summary is not the evidence that reveals it. Keep the three questions distinct rather than calling every change ‘the model got worse.’

Separate an operational report into what is observed and what is unresolved. More long-distance inputs support an input-distribution statement. Matched labels compared with the quality reference support an observed-error statement. Conditional-target evidence addresses whether the feature/label relationship changed. The absence of labels does not prove that quality stayed constant; it means the labeled-quality question is not yet measured by that evidence. Likewise, input drift does not prove that quality worsened. Keeping these distinctions preserves uncertainty without discarding useful distribution or service evidence, and prevents a response justified by one type of evidence from being mislabeled as another.

teaching_blocks.content: Do not use protected test observations to fit preprocessing, choose a model or tune its settings; doing so leaks information into the chosen system. teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the candidate has lower expected cost than the incumbent but fails a required slice check. Reject it under the fixed gate policy. Calculate both costs with the same supplied deployment probabilities, error costs and actual-class conditional rates. A missing conditioning group does not provide a defined rate. Keep protected-test observations out of fitting and setting choice. Bind the exact registry/artifact identity and verdict to the controlled promotion record, with assertion fixtures for accepted, boundary and failed cases. Approval evidence for candidate A must not be reused for candidate B just because both came from the same retraining pipeline.

The incumbent and candidate must be evaluated under the same fixed validation question before their expected costs are comparable. Keep quality, required slices and deployment compatibility as separately named gate results. A cost improvement does not erase a compatibility failure, and a complete gate record for one identity cannot be transferred to another. Accepted, boundary and rejected fixtures should verify both verdict and identity binding. teaching_blocks.content: Retrained does not mean accepted. An aggregate gain cannot bypass a required slice or compatibility gate, and validation of one artifact does not approve another.

Inspect the authorized instance before acting, record what failed and test the runbook's supported hypothesis. After start completes, reconnect and compare model-service state and endpoint behavior with the expected contract. A running instance state is a lifecycle observation; readiness and a successful bounded prediction are service observations. Retain both in the same recovery record along with authorized target identity. This verifies the supplied recovery procedure without assuming that a restart of an arbitrary resource would be safe or sufficient.

teaching_blocks.content: Retired resources can be cleaned up only after ownership and release status are verified. An old-looking container may still reference active artifacts, so age alone is not a safe authorization rule.

teaching_blocks.content: Compare actual container labels, identities, running/exit state and logs with the approved active/retired inventory and compute lifecycle. Stop and remove only a verified retired container. Delete only the exclusively retired nonproduction instance under the approved disk-preservation policy. teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Removing a retired container is not authorization to delete shared artifacts. Cleanup follows verified ownership, permitted scope and lifecycle state while preserving the active serving release.
